idiom_name: sealed interface Intent + record ViewState + switch reducer + Observable/Flow state stream
implementation_notes: The pattern's original realization was Java with RxJava: Dorfmann's MVI articles modelled intents as observables of user input, the model as an Observable<ViewState> emitted by the business logic, and the view as one render(viewState) plus the intent methods. Modern Java expresses the same loop with records for state and intent variants and a switch over the sealed intent type, which makes the reducer total and the variant set closed, while RxJava or java.util.concurrent.Flow carries the state stream to the view. The structure itself is still hand-assembled - no dominant Java MVI library exists - so the honest classification is manual; it is justified when a screen has many concurrent sub-states and must be replayed in tests, while a plain MVVM view model is less ceremony for simple screens.
pitfalls: Records are shallowly immutable: a List field aliases a mutable collection, so copy defensively (List.copyOf) when constructing states.
A state Observable that terminates on error kills the stream; MVI models failures as states (onErrorReturn/onErrorResumeNext), not as termination.
Subscribing on the wrong scheduler lets state emissions touch the view from a background thread; observeOn the UI scheduler and dispose subscriptions with the screen.
Nullable fields make 'not loaded', 'empty' and 'failed' indistinguishable; model the variants explicitly so the view cannot render contradictory flags.
